q: A butt marked for Fino loses its flor without ever being refortified, and finishes with the nose of an Amontillado over the body of an Oloroso. Which style is it?
exp: An Amontillado is refortified on purpose to kill its flor, while a Palo Cortado arrives there by accident. It carries the aromatic delicacy of the one over the body of an Oloroso, and it is the rarest of the dry styles.

q: A cellar hand fills a Sherry butt right up to the bung and is told to draw some back out. What has he got wrong?
opts: Full butts cannot be stacked safely in the bodega
The wine needs a headspace of air above it
It leaves no room for the sweetening wine added later
The wine expands as it warms and would burst the cask
exp: A 600-litre bota is filled to around 500 litres. The air above the wine is what keeps a film of flor alive on a Fino, and what feeds the slow oxidation of an Oloroso.

q: In a Sherry bodega, which row of butts is drawn from when wine is bottled?
opts: The solera, the row nearest the floor
The youngest criadera at the top
The first criadera, immediately above it
Whichever row the cellar master judges ready
exp: Solera comes from suelo, the floor. What is drawn off is replaced from the first criadera, which is replaced from the second, and so on upward, so no bottle is ever the produce of one year.

q: The letters VORS on a Sherry label promise an average age of what?
exp: VOS marks an average of twenty years and VORS thirty, both verified before the label may be used. They appear on the dry oxidative styles and on Pedro Ximenez, never on a Fino.

q: A bottle of Fino has stood open behind the bar for a fortnight. What has become of it?
opts: Nothing, since fortification makes it stable
It has opened up and improved with air
exp: Biologically aged Sherry is a light wine of about fifteen percent that has been shielded from oxygen its whole life. Treat an open bottle as you would an open white, replace it after a few days, and serve it cold in a proper glass.

q: Montilla-Moriles in Cordoba province supplies much of the raw material for one famous Andalucian sweet wine. Which grape ripens there for it?
exp: Montilla is hot enough to ripen Pedro Ximenez to enormous sugar, and the grapes are then sun-dried on mats before pressing. That raisined must is what sweetens a Cream Sherry.

q: Fine, persistent bead and a bready character in the glass point to a second fermentation carried out where?
opts: In a cask under a veil of yeast
In the same bottle the wine is sold in
exp: That is the traditional method, and the wine then rests on its spent yeast inside that bottle for a year or more. The pressure and the toasty flavour both come from there.

q: Gas is pumped into a finished still wine under pressure, exactly as it is into a soft drink. What gives that away in the glass?
opts: A coarse bubble that dies fast
A deeper colour and a heavier texture
A very fine and persistent bead
exp: Carbon dioxide made slowly by a fermentation under pressure leaves the wine in a fine, steady thread; gas pumped into a finished wine leaves it in a rush. It is the cheapest route to a bubble. The fizz froths up hard, feels aggressive in the mouth, and is gone inside a minute.

q: After the second fermentation the spent yeast has to be worked down into the neck of the bottle. What is that operation called?
exp: Remuage is the French name for it. Bottles are tilted and turned a fraction at a time, by hand on a pupitre or by machine in a gyropalette, until the sediment sits against the closure.

q: The neck of a bottle is dipped in freezing brine and a plug of ice is then blown out. Which step is that?
exp: Freezing traps the sediment in a pellet that the wine's own pressure expels the moment the cap comes off. The small loss of volume is what the dosage replaces.

q: Topping a bottle back up after disgorgement, with wine and a measured amount of sugar, goes by which name?
exp: The dosage, also called the liqueur d'expedition, sets the final sweetness and rounds off the acidity. The liqueur de tirage is the other end of the process, the sugar and yeast that began the second fermentation.

q: Quarter bottles and jeroboams are often filled from wine that fermented in an ordinary bottle, was emptied under pressure into a tank, filtered and bottled again. Which method is that?
exp: Riddling and disgorging an awkward format one bottle at a time is slow and wasteful, so the wine is decanted under pressure and the sediment filtered out instead. Because it leaves the bottle it fermented in, such a wine may be labelled bottle fermented but never traditional method.

q: Brioche, toast and biscuit aromas in a bottle-fermented sparkling wine arise from what?
exp: Autolysis is the breakdown of the dead yeast cells. Once the yeast has finished it dies and slowly ruptures, releasing compounds into the wine around it. The longer a bottle rests on those lees, the more pronounced the character.

q: A single fermentation is halted by cold and left to finish inside a sealed bottle, leaving the wine cloudy and lightly fizzy. Which technique is that?
exp: No fresh yeast or sugar is added for a second fermentation, so the bubbles come from the first one finishing in glass. It is the basis of pet-nat and of Bugey-Cerdon.

q: A label reading Blanc de Noirs tells the guest what?
opts: The wine is white but made from black grapes
Red and white wine were blended together
The wine spent time on its skins
The wine is white and made only from white grapes
exp: Gentle pressing draws the juice off before it picks up colour from the skins. Blanc de Blancs is the mirror image, white grapes alone.

q: An Italian label may say frizzante rather than spumante. What does that distinction record?
exp: Frizzante is lightly sparkling, roughly one to two and a half atmospheres, while spumante is fully sparkling above three. Moscato d'Asti is frizzante and Asti is spumante.
